En un sistema de dos masas acopladas, ca: In a system of two coupled masses, each pushes the other through the central spring, and the motions are not independent. But there are always two special ways of moving, the normal modes, in which both masses oscillate at once with the same frequency $ω$: $x_1 = a_1 cos(ω t)$ and $x_2 = a_2 cos(ω t)$. Substituting into the equations $m_1 x_1″ = −(k_1 + k_c) x_1 + k_c x_2$ and $m_2 x_2″ = k_c x_1 − (k_c + k_2) x_2$ gives a linear system whose solutions exist only if $(A − ω^2)(D − ω^2) − B C = 0$.
Con $m_1 = m_2 = m$ y $k_1 = k_2 = k$ lo: With $m_1 = m_2 = m$ and $k_1 = k_2 = k$ the modes are simple: in the first the masses move in phase, the central spring is not stretched and $ω_1 = √(k/m)$; in the second they move in antiphase and $ω_2 = √((k + 2 k_c)/m)$. Any motion is the sum of both, and so there are two constants of each kind (amplitude and phase) that are fixed by the four initial conditions.
Si se suelta solo una masa, se excitan l: If only one mass is released, both modes are excited equally and $x_1 = A cos((ω_2 − ω_1) t/2) cos((ω_1 + ω_2) t/2)$: the amplitude of each mass slowly rises and falls (the beat) while they oscillate quickly. The energy passes completely from one mass to the other every $π/(ω_2 − ω_1)$; with weak coupling the two frequencies are similar and the exchange is slow, as with two pendulums joined by a thread.
